title: Verifying Groups in Linear Time
authors: Shai Evra (The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel), Shay Gadot (The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel), Ohad Klein (The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel), Ilan Komargodski (The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel)
abstract: Consider the following problem: Given an $n \times n$ multiplication table, decide whether it is a Cayley multiplication table of a group. Among deterministic algorithms for this problem, the best known algorithm is implied by F. W. Light's associativity test (1949) and has running time of $O(n^2 \log n)$. Allowing randomization, the best known algorithm has running time of $O(n^2 \log (1/\delta))$, where $\delta>0$ is the error probability of the algorithm (Rajagopalan and Schulman, FOCS 1996, SICOMP 2000). In this work, we improve upon both of the above known algorithms. Specifically, we present a deterministic algorithm for the above problem whose running time is $O(n^2)$. This performance is optimal up to constants. A central tool we develop is an efficient algorithm for finding a subset $A$ of a group $G$ satisfying $A^2=G$ while $|A| = O(\sqrt{|G|})$.

Since the input in this problem consists of an n × n
multiplication table of group elements, it is obvious
that every algorithm for the above problem must run
in time Ω(n2 ). What about upper bounds?
Testing for the existence of an identity element and
verifying that each element has an inverse can both be
trivially done in time O(n2 ) by brute force. The nontrivial task is testing associativity, i.e., that for every
a, b, c ∈ G it holds that (a · b) · c = a · (b · c). A
brute-force algorithm would require Θ(n3 ) time. An
observation attributed to F. W. Light in 1949 (see [1])
is that it suffices to test associativity only for all triples
a, b, c such that a, c ∈ G but b ∈ R, where R is
a set of generators of G. Furthermore, it is possible
to deterministically compute a set of generators of
size ⌊log n⌋ in O(n2 ) time [2]. Thus, we can already
improve upon the brute force approach and get a
deterministic algorithm running in time O(n2 log n).
A classical work of Rajagopalan and Schulman [2]
studied the general problem of testing associativity
of a given relation (regardless of the existence of
identity and inverses). They showed that an arbitrary
relation · as above can be tested for associativity
using a randomized algorithm that has complexity
O(n2 log(1/δ)), where δ > 0 is the error probability
of the algorithm. This implies a randomized algorithm
for group checking1 with complexity O(n2 log(1/δ))
and δ probability of error. This complexity is better
than the one implied by Light’s observation for rather
large values of δ; for instance, if we settle for small
constant non-zero probability of error, the complexity
